On a trip to the seaside you spot a white conch shell on the beach, pick it up and hold it to your ear, and hear something that sounds like waves. Why?

Some say the sea has tucked its stories inside and wants to whisper them to us.

Others say no: what’s inside is the shell’s longing for the sea, and its memories of it.

Whether or not they’re right, they are certainly poetic and romantic.

Now here is how a hopelessly unromantic guy answers the question:

He does kill the mood a bit, but he is basically right. The shell picks up the sounds around it and amplifies them by resonance. Note, though, that the amplified sound is not the sound of our own blood flowing: people who listened before and after exercise heard no real difference. What gets amplified is just the sound of moving air, in other words the wind.

At this point someone might ask: even in a quiet room with no wind, you still hear something like waves when you hold a shell to your ear. Why?

Mainly because the air in a room is never completely still. Every room has a background of white noise that we don’t usually notice. If you don’t believe it, cup your hands over your ears right now and you’ll hear it, more clearly still on a quiet night.

Who the hell made this white-noise GIF? So much for “friendly.”

Broadband white noise is fairly friendly to people. We don’t find it disturbing, and the brain sometimes “filters it out” automatically so that we stop noticing it. It can also mask other noises, which is why many people who struggle to fall asleep use it as a sleep aid. (For more on masking, see our earlier posts A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1 and A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2.)

But I digress. Back to the shell: it amplifies sound because it is a Helmholtz resonator, which is what this article is really about.

Hermann von Helmholtz was a great nineteenth-century German physicist and physiologist (he also appeared in our earlier post A history of acoustics: architectural acoustics). He designed and named the Helmholtz resonator in 1850. His original purpose was to pick out sounds of particular frequencies and pitches from complex noise or music, a bit like a spectrum analyzer.

Helmholtz resonators

Its structure is very simple: a cavity with an opening, fitted with a short neck, where the area of the opening is much smaller than the surface area of the cavity.

The resonator’s sound comes from the vibration of the air column in the neck. When a disturbance outside pushes the air column a little way into the cavity, it compresses the air inside and raises the pressure. The higher pressure pushes the air column back out. When it gets back to its starting point, inertia carries it a little farther outward, which lets the air in the cavity expand and lowers the pressure, and that pressure difference pulls the air column back in. As long as the outside disturbance keeps going, the air column in the neck keeps oscillating back and forth, and the resonator sounds.

The air in the cavity acts like a spring and the air column in the neck like a mass, so the resonator can be modeled as a single-degree-of-freedom vibrating system. One condition for this equivalence is that the wavelength of the sound must be much larger than the resonator.

Theory gives the natural frequency of the resonator as:

Here f0 is the lowest resonance frequency of the Helmholtz resonator, c is the speed of sound, S is the cross-sectional area of the neck, d is its diameter, l is its length and V is the volume of the cavity. The second term in the denominator under the square root, 0.8d, is an end correction to the neck length. It accounts for the mass of air that actually vibrates, which includes not just the air column inside the neck but also some of the air just outside it. When the frequency of the outside excitation matches the resonator’s natural frequency, resonance occurs and sound at that frequency is amplified. This is the so-called Helmholtz resonance principle.

A Helmholtz resonator is a highly efficient device for converting sound energy that needs no power source of its own and is driven entirely by outside vibration. It has a wide range of uses. Line the cavity with sound-absorbing material and it becomes a resonant absorber that soaks up a great deal of sound at its natural frequency.

Perforated wall panels

Perforated ceiling panels

In some buildings you will often see walls or ceilings covered with flat panels full of small holes. These perforated panels are usually mounted some distance from the wall, and each hole together with the space behind it forms a Helmholtz resonator. They absorb sound, reduce reverberation in the room and improve its acoustics.

The video below also shows nicely how well resonant absorbers work. Anyone renovating their home at the moment should take a good look.

High-rise flats along busy streets or near highways have great views, but they are often plagued by noise. Closing the windows solves the problem but cuts off the fresh air. (Commenter: “Just install a ventilation system!” Answer: “Can’t afford it!”)

Is there a window that cuts noise and still lets air through? Yes! The “giant perforated panel” window in the video does exactly that, taking the noise from 73 dB straight down to 54 dB! You know you want one.

It uses the latest, most cutting-edge acoustic metamaterial technology (a.k.a. drilling holes)!

Resonant absorbers like these are also widely used to treat intake and exhaust noise in cars with combustion engines.

Besides the sea in a seashell, Helmholtz resonance explains plenty of everyday phenomena. For example, when you pour boiling water into a thermos flask or fill a vacuum mug from a hot-water tap, you can usually tell by ear when it is nearly full. The sound from the flask or mug changes as the water level rises. Why?

The resonator formula makes everything clear. As the water rises, the air volume V in the flask or mug shrinks, so the resonance frequency f0 rises. When the sound turns from dull to brighter and brighter, we know the vessel is almost full and take a little more care not to scald ourselves.

Bet there are goji berries in there! (Goji-berry tea in a thermos is China’s classic middle-aged health drink.)

When you are driving or riding in a car, opening a side window or the sunroof just a little can sometimes cause a tremendous noise. This is known as side-window or sunroof buffeting, or “wind throb.” It, too, is caused by Helmholtz resonance. With a side window or sunroof open, the whole passenger cabin becomes one big Helmholtz resonator. When the frequency of the outside excitation coincides with the natural frequency of the cabin-resonator, the cabin fills with an enormous noise.

How the interior sound spectrum changes with vehicle speed when the sunroof is open

After all that, back to where we started.

And yet who can deny that the sound of the waves is the shell’s endless longing for the sea it left behind, and its deepest memory of home?

Perhaps not even Herr Helmholtz.
